pos: adj. (excessively concerned with minor details, technical rules, or displays of learning); pedant, n.; pedantry, n.; pedantically, adv.
etymology: From French pédant, from Italian pedante, “a teacher, schoolmaster”; its earlier origin is uncertain. In early English a pedant was simply a schoolmaster, and the word soured into a name for the man who parades the schoolroom. Related forms: pedant (n.), pedantry (n.), pedantically (adv.).
biblical_def: Pedantic describes the man excessively concerned with minor details, technical rules, or displays of learning, especially when that concern obscures the main point or practical purpose. In plain English: getting so caught up in proving every little point that you miss what actually matters. The word is not biblical, but the fault is, and the Lord names it in the scribes and Pharisees: “ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Mat 23:23). He gives it its picture: “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” (Mat 23:24). Yet in the same breath He adds, “these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone” (Mat 23:23). The lesser duty was not the sin; the lost proportion was. Paul charges the church “that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” (2Ti 2:14), and in the next breath commands the opposite of carelessness: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). Precision is not pedantry. A detail matters when it changes the truth, meaning, safety, or outcome. Pedantry gives minor distinctions more weight than their purpose warrants, or uses knowledge to display superiority rather than help someone understand, for “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1Co 8:1). Neither passage excuses false teaching or makes careful study a fault.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pedantic as ostentatious of learning; vainly displaying or making a show of knowledge; applied to persons or things.
webster_full: PEDANT'IC, PEDANT'ICAL, a. Ostentatious of learning; vainly displaying or making a show of knowledge; applied to persons or things; as a pedantic writer or scholar; a pedantic description or expression.
PED'ANTRY, n. Vain ostentation of learning; a boastful display of knowledge of any kind.
Pedantry is the unseasonable ostentation of learning.
scriptures: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.
Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
corruption_summary: Two errors sit on either side of the word: the pedant who loses the weightier matters in the small ones, and the careless man who calls every needed distinction pedantry.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has widened since Webster, from a vain display of learning to an excessive concern with minor rules and details, but the widening is honest, and both senses describe the same fault: knowledge or exactness put to the service of the self rather than the truth or the neighbor. The principle to recover is proportion. The Lord did not rebuke the Pharisees for tithing herbs; He said “these ought ye to have done” (Mat 23:23). He rebuked them for weighing the gnat with care and the camel not at all.

The live misuse runs the other way. Pedantic is a convenient word to throw at anyone who insists that a word of Scripture or a clause of a confession means what it says. That is not pedantry. A distinction that changes the truth, meaning, safety, or outcome is precision, and the man “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) is doing a workman's duty. The test is purpose: does the correction serve the hearer's understanding, or the corrector's standing? Strife about words “to no profit” subverts the hearers (2Ti 2:14); careful study that serves them is commanded in the very next verse.
roots_summary: Greek diulizo (G1368), to strain out; barus (G926), heavy, weighty; logomachia (G3055), a battle about words.
roots_lines: Greek diulizo (G1368) — to strain, filter out; Matthew 23:24, the gnat strained out of the cup.
Greek barus (G926) — heavy, weighty; the weightier matters of the law, Matthew 23:23.
Greek logomachia (G3055) — a battle of words; 1 Timothy 6:4, with its cognate verb in 2 Timothy 2:14.
English pedant — first a schoolmaster, then one who makes a show of the schoolroom.
English pedantry — in Webster 1828, the unseasonable ostentation of learning.
usage: He gave a pedantic correction of the speaker's grammar but never addressed the speaker's argument.
Precision is not pedantry: a detail matters when it changes the truth, meaning, safety, or outcome.
“Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” — the test of every correction.
